subject: Critical Thinking
title: Negotiation as Structured Argument
description: A quick win: understand Negotiation as Structured Argument.

hook.text: A hostage negotiator walks into a crisis. She never raises her voice once.

buildup.text: Negotiation is argument with stakes. Both sides present positions, but the goal is agreement, not victory.

discovery.text: The best negotiators use principled argumentation: separate people from problems, focus on interests not positions.

twist.text: Harvard's Getting to Yes framework shows that hard bargaining loses to collaborative reasoning in repeated games.

climax.text: BATNA — your Best Alternative to Agreement — is the hidden argument that gives you real power.

punchline.text: The strongest argument is a good backup plan.

quiz.question: What does BATNA stand for in negotiation theory?
options: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement

details.summary: Negotiation is argumentation with stakes. Both sides present reasons for their positions, make concessions, and seek mutually acceptable conclusions. Understanding argument structure makes you a better negotiator.
details.whyItMatters: Salary talks, business deals, and diplomatic agreements all depend on structured reasoning. Better arguments mean better outcomes.
takeaways: Negotiation applies argument structure to real-world stakes
BATNA (best alternative) strengthens your argumentative position
Win-win outcomes require finding shared premises

faq.question: How does knowing your BATNA improve your negotiating arguments?
faq.answer: Your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement sets your minimum threshold. Knowing it means you argue from confidence rather than desperation, and you can walk away from bad deals.

faq.question: What argumentative technique is most useful in salary negotiation?
faq.answer: Anchoring with strong evidence. Present market data for your role before numbers are discussed. The first well-supported figure sets the frame for the entire negotiation.
